result: The authors claim that steroids drive mRNA synthesis through frequency modulation of transcription, where digital behavior in single cells gives rise to analog dose response at the population level. The response element controls the frequency of gene activity but not the duration or rate of transcription during active periods.
status_reasoning: Reviewers acknowledged the technical novelty but noted that 'in spite of the technical novelty the main conclusions of this work mostly confirmed previous observations indicating that the on-off states are digital in nature.' They asked authors to 'clarify the novelty of their findings in the context of prior knowledge,' suggesting uncertainty about whether these findings represent a significant advance beyond what was already known.

result: The authors report that at 50 μM PA, the average on duration is 36 ± 6 min and off duration is 35 ± 4 min, with both exponentially distributed. The time between on-states decreased at higher doses of PA, while the duration of the active state and transcription rate were invariant with dose.
status_reasoning: Reviewers requested critical missing baseline data: 'Figures 2I and 2J. It is necessary to show the data with 0 micromolar PA. This is the baseline control.' They also asked whether 'analyses, such as those in Figure 2E–J, carried out for each clonal cell line to confirm for each the dose-dependent off-time and dose-independent on-time,' indicating uncertainty about the generalizability and completeness of these measurements.

result: The authors claim that transcription kinetics depend strongly on transgene insertion site, with three clones showing different maximum mRNA levels but similar EC50 values and Hill coefficients. The dose-dependent activation rate and dose-independent inactivation rate remain invariant across insertion sites, but the initiation rate changes with cell line.
status_reasoning: Reviewers raised concerns about the interpretation of clonal variation: 'Were analyses, such as those in Figure 2E–J, carried out for each clonal cell line to confirm for each the dose-dependent off-time and dose-independent on-time? (It is not apparent if Figure 2 shows data from one clonal cell line or the averages of all three clonal lines.)' This indicates uncertainty about whether the claimed invariance of certain parameters across clones was actually demonstrated.

result: The authors report that a single pulse of active ligand resulted in a burst of polymerase activity several hours later (average 106 ± 36 min delay), with 70% of activated cells showing a single on-state. They conclude that one dose of transcription factor yields one cycle of transcription.
status_reasoning: Reviewers expressed significant concerns about the photoactivation experiments: 'Were there multiple on-periods in the other 30% of activated cells? Authors should show statistical analyses of the probabilities of single or multiple cycles occurring from a single transient hormone dose. Additionally the average, maximum, and minimum on-periods should be calculated and presented for this experiment and compared to steady state hormone dosing assays.' They also questioned whether 'the PA that is released upon UV treatment exists only transiently because it becomes blocked by an excess of caged PA' and asked authors to 'prove this point.'

result: The authors characterize a photoactivatable ligand that acts as an antagonist in the caged state and an agonist in the uncaged state, with competition experiments showing fivefold reduction in protein levels at 100 μM DMNB-PA.
status_reasoning: Reviewers questioned the mechanism and interpretation: 'It appears that the authors presume that the PA that is released upon UV treatment exists only transiently because it becomes blocked by an excess of caged PA. Is this what the authors mean to suggest? If so, can they prove this point?' This indicates uncertainty about the authors' interpretation of how the caged compound functions in the experimental system.

result: The authors report that the duration of the active transcriptional state is on the order of an hour, with a delay between photoactivation and transcription site appearance comparable to the off period. They attribute this to chromatin remodeling, noting that non-chromatinized templates showed rapid induction (<20 min).
status_reasoning: Reviewers directly challenged this interpretation: 'It is unclear why the first transcription sites are only visible several hours after induction. Opening of chromatin of a single copy gene should not impose such a large delay between docking of the active ligand-receptor complex and subsequent RNA synthesis. Is this a result of the complexity of the reporter system? How well does this reflect the induction of endogenous steroid regulated genes? This can be easily tested by in situ hybridization.' This indicates significant uncertainty about whether the observed delay reflects biological chromatin remodeling or artifacts of the reporter system.

result: The authors report observations of transcriptional bursting using live-cell microscopy and FISH, showing dose-dependent heterogeneity in mRNA distribution across cells, with individual mRNA appearing as diffraction-limited puncta and active transcription sites as bright nuclear spots.
status_reasoning: Reviewers raised serious concerns about cell health that could affect interpretation: 'The cells in Figures 3 and 6 look sick. In particular, the nuclear blebbing and irregularly shaped nuclei are indicative of apoptosis. This needs to be examined carefully as it could alter the interpretation of the data.' They also required DNA damage controls: 'Exposing cells, and in particular nuclei, to 349nm light can result in DNA damage. Labeling with γ-H2A.X must be done +/- uncaging to be sure that the observed results are not influenced by DNA damage.'

result: The authors describe their experimental system consisting of an ecdysone receptor-controlled reporter gene visualized using MS2 RNA labeling and FISH approaches, with a bi-cistronic construct introduced via lentivirus infection.
status_reasoning: Reviewers questioned fundamental aspects of the system: 'Can the authors confirm that there is only one transcription site per cell? Is this single transcription site stably maintained through multiple generations?' This indicates uncertainty about the basic characteristics of the experimental system and whether it represents a single-copy integration as assumed.

result: The authors apply the Random Telegraph model to their data, claiming that the gene exists in inactive and active states, with only the activation rate varying with dose while other parameters remain constant.
status_reasoning: Reviewers identified confusion in the model presentation: 'In Figure 4C, is the x-axis equal to time? If so, wouldn't (a) and (b) be times rather than rates? Also, would the fraction of time in the active state be equal to (b)/(b)+(a)? Please clarify the formulas as well as the use of the terms "rate" vs "time" in this section.' This indicates uncertainty about whether the model is correctly formulated and applied.

result: The authors claim that episomal genes do not show frequency modulation and that frequency of initiation determines RNA levels only when the gene is integrated into chromatin.
status_reasoning: While reviewers did not directly challenge this claim, their concern about whether the long delay reflects 'the complexity of the reporter system' and request to test 'endogenous steroid regulated genes' by 'in situ hybridization' suggests uncertainty about whether the chromatin-dependent frequency modulation observed in this artificial system reflects natural gene regulation.
